transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya, Jonah (Redwood); Dr. Elena Ruiz, Samir Gupta, Priya Menon (Vanguard)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account, and Jonah our solutions engineer is here too. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Elena: Doing well, thanks. Busy week but excited to chat.
[00:15] Jonah: Great to meet you all. Quick agenda - understand your infra constraints, security needs, and the network setup for a private deployment. We'll cover peering, private endpoints, region constraints, and what a pilot might look like.
[00:30] Samir: Sounds good. To frame things - Vanguard runs in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 primarily. We have some strict egress rules, and we need anything LLM-related to live inside our VPC or via private endpoints. No public internet egress for inference traffic ideally.
[00:50] Priya: Also need SOC2 coverage, audit logs, and KMS integration for keys. We talked to a few providers and want to see how Redwood handles private deployments.
[01:05] Maya: Totally. A lot to cover. Quick question - when you say no public egress, do you mean the inference nodes must be in your VPC (private) or you can accept provider-hosted but with a private endpoint/peering?
[01:20] Elena: Prefer the nodes inside our VPC or a VPC peered/dedicated in our account. We have strict data residency controls and our legal folks prefer us to manage the network.
[01:35] Jonah: Understood. We support a few deployment patterns: 1) Private deployment in your VPC - customer-managed nodes (we provide an install bundle and control plane) 2) VPC peering to Redwood-managed private VPC with tight peering and routing controls 3) Dedicated reserved capacity with PrivateLink endpoints. Each has tradeoffs.
[01:55] Samir: Can you expand on peering vs PrivateLink? We have transit gateways and prefer centralized routing.
[02:10] Jonah: Sure. With VPC peering or TGW attachments, you get direct routing but you need to handle route tables and ensure no overlapping CIDRs. PrivateLink (interface endpoints) means we expose an ENI in your subnet; traffic goes over AWS private network to Redwood's service endpoints. PrivateLink is easier for network isolation and avoids some routing complexity but can be a bit more costly and you don't own the compute.
[02:40] Priya: Does PrivateLink allow full egress control? We need to ensure keys never leave our control.
[02:50] Jonah: For keys KMS integration is supported. You can use your KMS or HSM for encryption at rest; we can also set up envelope encryption so the keys remain customer-controlled. For egress - with PrivateLink, traffic sits on AWS backbone and doesn't go public; audit logs are retained and can be forwarded to your S3 or SIEM.
[03:15] Elena: If we wanted compute in our account, how does Redwood handle updates and rollback? We want the runtime patched and maintained.
[03:25] Jonah: In that install model (private in your VPC), we run an operator that lets Redwood orchestrate runtime updates, but customers can restrict auto-updates. We support canary rollouts, pinned versions, and offline upgrade windows to meet your change control.
[03:45] Maya: Quick interjection, for many customers the Dedicated option - reserved capacity in a customer-dedicated pool - gives predictable latency and we can offer placement in specific regions. But for strict compliance you mentioned, private VPC install is the easiest to justify.
[04:05] Samir: Cost wise, does private install mean they pay for infra plus Redwood license?
[04:12] Maya: Yes. Private is typically a subscription plus the customer's infra. Dedicated (Redwood-managed but isolated) is a committed seat model. Hosted is usage-based. We'll send a pricing comparison.
[04:30] Elena: Region question - we need inference to be in eu-west-1 for EU data. Can Redwood pin region for private installs?
[04:42] Jonah: Absolutely. For private installs we deploy into the regions you specify. For Dedicated pools we can reserve capacity in particular regions, but some provider-managed fallbacks might exist. We can talk SLAs per region.
[04:58] Priya: About network ranges - we have overlapping CIDRs in some legacy accounts. How do you handle overlaps?
[05:08] Jonah: Overlaps are the main pain. If CIDR overlap, PrivateLink avoids that because you don't add routes; for peering/TGW we need unique ranges. If necessary, we can deploy in a transit VPC and NAT, but that's more complex. We recommend customers share CIDR ranges and we'll validate during onboarding.
[05:30] Samir: Do you support multi-region failover? Like primary in eu-west, failover in us-east?
[05:38] Jonah: Yes, we support cross-region replication of model artifacts and KV cache warmup strategies. For low RTOs we can set up cross-region active/standby with automated failover, but latency when failing over will depend on distance and cross-region traffic.
[05:55] Elena: Latency is a concern. Our SLAs are 100ms p50 and p95 under 300ms for synchronous calls. Can you get us numbers?
[06:05] Jonah: We'll run benchmarks, but typical p50 with dedicated GPU-backed endpoints in the same AZ is sub-80ms for small models; for large models or longer contexts it'll be higher. For private installs inside your VPC we avoid NAT hops and internet egress which helps. We'll provide realistic numbers in the follow-up.
[06:25] Maya: Another note - caching prefix/KV can dramatically reduce per-token cost for repeated contexts. If your workload is chatty, caching is worth discussing in the pilot.
[06:40] Samir: For network security, do you support SAML for SSO into the console and RBAC?
[06:47] Maya: Yes. We support SAML/SSO, SCIM for user provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC. For private deployments you can opt for a private control plane or a hybrid control plane; control plane network access can be restricted as well.
[07:05] Priya: Audit logs - retention and forward to our SIEM?
[07:10] Jonah: Yes. Logs can be forwarded to your S3 or to an HTTP endpoint, we have integration hooks; retention is configurable. We also integrate with cloud trail for activity logs in managed setups.
[07:25] Elena: Any compliance docs we can get?
[07:28] Maya: We'll send our SOC2 report, penetration test summary, and the network security whitepaper after this call.
[07:35] Samir: Good. On network egress - do you support Egress filter rules so inference nodes cannot make arbitrary outbound connections?
[07:44] Jonah: Yes, you can restrict egress via security groups and egress ACLs. In private install you control those; in PrivateLink we control the backend but we support strict egress policies and can validate via our pen tests.
[08:00] Elena: For pilot scope - we'd like to run a 2-week pilot: 1) baseline latency/cost with 2 models, 2) run through our SSO + audit flows, 3) test peering vs PrivateLink. Is that feasible?
[08:15] Maya: Totally feasible. Typical pilot is 2-4 weeks. Jonah, we can propose the benchmark and setup.
[08:20] Jonah: I'll draft a pilot plan. We'll need your CIDR ranges, the exact VPCs to peer, sample prompts, and target RPS. Also which models you want - open models or Redwood-curated ones?
[08:35] Samir: Start with a smaller curated model for latency tests then a larger one for quality. Target RPS 200 sustained, spikes 1k.
[08:45] Jonah: Got it. For 200 RPS sustained we'll design the instance types; I'll provide a cost estimate for infra.
[08:55] Maya: Quick note about canary/fallbacks - we have routing policies so if dedicated capacity is unavailable in a region we can fail to a compatible variant or degrade gracefully. That's often useful for resilience.
[09:10] Elena: We also use HSM for key storage. Any Redwood integration?
[09:15] Jonah: Yes, we support customer-managed HSM/KMS for encryption. We can integrate with AWS CloudHSM or partner HSMs via KMS. Keys never leave your control in envelope encryption mode.
[09:30] Priya: Auditing who accessed models is important for us. Can we get token-level traces?
[09:36] Jonah: Yes - per-token tracing and request-level audit trails are available in the console and can be exported. We'll include the retention options in the docs.
[09:50] Elena: Any networking templates you can share for CloudFormation/Terraform?
[09:55] Maya: Yes, we'll share Terraform templates and a network checklist for onboarding.
[10:05] Samir: A couple edge cases - do you require changes to our route tables or do you support AWS PrivateLink only? We prefer minimal routing changes.
[10:15] Jonah: If you want minimal changes PrivateLink is the lowest friction. For performance we sometimes recommend TGW peering if you already use transit gateway and want fine-grained control. We'll document both options.
[10:30] Elena: About data residency - if we pin to eu-west, are any metadata logs or control plane calls sent to other regions?
[10:40] Jonah: We can configure the control plane to be customer-managed or hybrid. For strict residency we run the private control plane in your region; otherwise some meta telemetry may route through the nearest control plane but we can opt out and keep everything local for Private deployments. We'll clarify in the security pack.
[11:05] Priya: How do you handle service accounts / least privilege for the operator?
[11:10] Jonah: Operator runs with a minimal set of IAM roles; we'll provide principle-of-least-privilege templates. You can also run the operator in a dedicated admin account.
[11:25] Elena: Ok, sounds promising. For timeline - we have a vendor selection committee next week and would like security docs and pricing by Monday. Can you get that?
[11:33] Maya: Yes - we'll send SOC2, pen test summary, pricing, and a pilot proposal by Monday.
[11:40] Samir: One last quick question: any hard limits on number of private endpoints or throughput per endpoint?
[11:48] Jonah: For PrivateLink endpoints AWS has ENI limits per AZ but we can recommend scaling across multiple subnets/AZs. Throughput depends on instance sizing; we'll give guidance in the estimate.
[12:05] Maya: Great - recap and next steps: We'll (1) send security docs and pricing, (2) Jonah will send pilot plan and latency/cost estimates, (3) Samir to share CIDRs and compliance checklist.
[12:20] Elena: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[12:25] Maya: Thanks all, talk soon.

(Transcript notes: occasional transcription artifacts - e.g., product names misheard as 'Redwood ded' or 'private link' sometimes spaced. Speakers overlap briefly at ~08:20.)
